lessons.title: Lesson 1: Food groups with local foods
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort the foods sold in your market into energy, body-building and protective food groups.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of foods sold in your market, you will sort local foods into energy, body-building and protective food groups, getting at least 8 of 10 right.
No single food gives the body everything it needs. An easy way to remember is three groups. Energy foods ("go" foods) give strength: maize, rice, millet, sorghum, cassava, yam, plantain, sweet potato, bread, and also oil. Body-building foods ("grow" foods) build muscles and blood: beans, lentils, cowpeas, groundnuts, eggs, fish, meat, chicken and milk. Protective foods ("glow" foods) help fight sickness: vegetables and fruit.
Local examples: in Kenya, ugali (energy), githeri or omena (body-building) and sukuma wiki (protective). In Nigeria, garri or yam (energy), beans or egusi (body-building) and ugu or bitter leaf (protective). In Ghana, banku or kenkey (energy), fish or groundnut soup (body-building) and kontomire (protective). In Senegal, rice or millet with niébé (cowpeas) and vegetables. In Egypt, bread with ful (fava beans) and salad.
Some foods are special helpers. Dark green leaves (amaranth, cassava leaves, moringa, kontomire) and orange foods (orange sweet potato, pawpaw, mango, carrots) are rich in vitamins. Beans, small dried fish, eggs, liver and dark green leaves give iron, which prevents anaemia.
Step by step:
- Write the foods your household ate yesterday.
- Mark each one: energy, body-building or protective.
- See which group is missing or small.
- Name one local food you can add for that group.
Words to know:
- Food group: foods that do a similar job in the body.
- Staple: the main filling food eaten most days, such as ugali, rice, garri or bread.
- Anaemia: weak blood, often from too little iron; it makes people tired and weak.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Healthy diet (fruit and vegetables, salt, sugar and fat)
- WHO fact sheet: Anaemia (who is at risk, iron-rich foods, foods that block iron)
Try it now: Write everything your household ate yesterday. Mark each food E (energy), B (body-building) or P (protective). Circle the group you ate least, and write one local food you could add tomorrow.
You can now sort local foods into energy, body-building and protective groups and spot what is missing.

check.q: Which of these is a body-building food?
check.why: Beans are rich in protein, which builds the body.

check.q: A family in Accra ate banku and pepper sauce all day. Which group is missing most?
check.why: Banku is an energy food; the meal needs fish or beans and vegetables.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Building a balanced plate
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a balanced plate with a staple, a body-building food and vegetables or fruit.
This lesson builds toward: Given the foods in your kitchen, you will plan a balanced plate with a staple, a body-building food and vegetables or fruit, with vegetables or fruit filling about half the plate.
A simple guide for each main meal: about half the plate vegetables and fruit, about a quarter a staple, and about a quarter a body-building food. You do not need a real plate; think of the bowl or the shared tray in the same parts.
WHO advises adults to eat at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day, which is about five handfuls. Leaves cooked in a soup or stew count. Whole grains and less-refined foods, such as brown rice, millet, sorghum or whole maize flour, keep you full for longer.
Make small changes, not a new kitchen. Add a handful of greens to the stew. Add beans to the rice (waakye in Ghana, rice and beans in Nigeria, githeri in Kenya). Add a small piece of fish or an egg for the children. Eat a fruit in season instead of a sweet snack.
To help the body use iron from beans and greens, eat them with a vitamin C food such as tomatoes, oranges, guava or mango. Drink tea or coffee between meals, not with them, because they make iron harder to take in.
Step by step:
- Picture the plate in four parts.
- Fill about half with vegetables and fruit.
- Fill about a quarter with a staple.
- Fill about a quarter with a body-building food.
- Add a vitamin C food; keep tea for between meals.
Words to know:
- Balanced: a meal with the right mix of food groups.
- Whole grain: grain with the outer layer kept, such as brown rice, millet or whole maize flour.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Healthy diet (fruit and vegetables, salt, sugar and fat)
- WHO fact sheet: Anaemia (who is at risk, iron-rich foods, foods that block iron)
Try it now: Plan tomorrow's main meal using foods you already have. Draw the plate (or bowl) and write what goes in each part. Add one vitamin C food.
You can now plan a balanced plate with a staple, a body-building food and plenty of vegetables or fruit.

check.q: On a balanced plate, about how much should be vegetables and fruit?
check.why: About half the plate vegetables and fruit is the simple guide.

check.q: Why eat tomatoes or an orange with beans and greens?
options: They help the body take in iron
They make the food last longer
check.why: Vitamin C helps the body use iron from plant foods.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Less salt, sugar and oil, and safe food
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Change a recipe to use less salt, sugar and oil and apply the five keys to safer food.
This lesson builds toward: Given a household recipe or meal, you will change the recipe to use less salt, sugar and oil and apply the WHO five keys to safer food, naming at least two changes and the five keys.
Too much salt raises blood pressure, which can lead to stroke and heart disease. WHO advises adults to eat less than 5 grams of salt a day, just under one level teaspoon, counting all the salt in stock cubes, seasoning powders, salted fish and bread. Use less salt and fewer cubes, and add taste with onion, garlic, ginger, pepper and herbs. If you use salt, choose iodized salt.
Sugar: WHO advises keeping free sugars (sugar added to food and drinks, and sugar in honey, sodas and juices) to less than 10% of daily energy, and less is better. For most adults that is less than about 12 level teaspoons a day. Sweet tea, sodas and juice add up fast. Oil: use a little, and fry less often; boil, steam or stew instead.
Food safety stops diarrhoea and food poisoning. WHO's five keys to safer food: keep clean (wash hands and surfaces); separate raw and cooked food; cook thoroughly, especially meat, fish and eggs; keep food at safe temperatures (do not leave cooked food out for hours); and use safe water and fresh, safe foods.
These rules matter even more if you sell cooked food, because one mistake can make many customers sick.
Step by step:
- Count the salt, cubes and sugar in one usual recipe.
- Cut each by a little, and add onion, garlic, pepper or herbs.
- Choose to stew or boil instead of frying once a week.
- Check the recipe against the five keys to safer food.
Words to know:
- Iodized salt: salt with iodine added, which the body needs.
- Free sugars: sugar added to food and drinks, plus sugar in honey, syrups and fruit juices.
- Food poisoning: sickness from eating food with germs or poison in it.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Healthy diet (fruit and vegetables, salt, sugar and fat)
- WHO: Five keys to safer food manual
Try it now: Take one dish your household eats often, such as jollof rice, egusi soup, thieboudienne or a bean stew. Write two changes that cut salt, sugar or oil, and one food safety key you will practise when cooking it.
You can now change a recipe to use less salt, sugar and oil and keep food safe with the five keys.

check.q: Which change cuts salt in a stew?
options: Add salted fish and more salt
Use fewer cubes and add onion, garlic and pepper
check.why: Cubes and seasoning powders are salty; herbs and spices add taste without salt.

check.q: Which is one of WHO's five keys to safer food?
options: Keep cooked food out all day
Use the same board for raw meat and salad without washing
Taste raw meat to check it
check.why: Separating raw and cooked foods stops germs spreading.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Eating well on a budget

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Comparing food prices for value
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare the cost of foods in the same group to find better value.
This lesson builds toward: Using prices from your own market, you will compare the cost of foods for the same food group to find better value, choosing the cheaper option that gives the same nutrients, with the sums correct.
Good food does not have to cost more. The trick is to compare foods that do the same job. For body-building foods, compare beans, lentils, cowpeas, groundnuts, eggs, small dried fish and meat by what one family meal of each costs. Beans and small fish often give a lot for little money.
How to compare: write the price and the amount you get, then work out the cost for one family meal. Example (made-up numbers, not real prices): a cup of dried beans costs NGN 600 and feeds the family once; meat for the same meal costs NGN 3,000. The beans are five times cheaper for that meal. Use your own market's prices; they change with the season.
Ways to save: buy fruit and vegetables in season, when they are cheapest. Buy dry foods (beans, grains, dried fish) in bigger amounts with neighbours or your savings group and share. Grow leaves such as amaranth, kale, moringa or spinach in a small garden, a sack or a tin. Cut back on sodas, sweets and packet snacks, which cost a lot and give little.
Do not waste: store dry foods in closed, dry containers away from damp and pests, and use leftovers safely the next day.
Step by step:
- Pick one food group, for example body-building foods.
- Write the price and amount for three foods in that group.
- Work out the cost for one family meal of each.
- Choose the best value, and note which foods are in season.
Words to know:
- Value: how much good food you get for your money.
- In season: the time of year when a crop is harvested, so it is plentiful and cheaper.
Try it now: At your market or shop, write the price and amount for three body-building foods (for example beans, eggs and dried fish). Work out the cost for one family meal of each with your phone calculator. Circle the best value. Write the currency (KES, NGN, GHS, XOF, MAD or yours).
You can now compare food prices by cost per meal and pick the best value in each food group.

check.q: What is the fairest way to compare beans and meat?
options: The cost for one family meal of each
check.why: Cost per meal compares what you really get for the money.

check.q: Example only: beans for one meal cost XOF 500 and fish for one meal costs XOF 1,500. How many times cheaper are the beans?

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Feeding young children and pregnant or breastfeeding women
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan one day's meals for a young child or a pregnant or breastfeeding woman following WHO advice.
This lesson builds toward: For a child aged 6 to 23 months, or a pregnant or breastfeeding woman, you will plan one day's meals that meet WHO feeding advice, with the right number of meals for the child's age, or extra iron-rich food for the woman.
Young children grow fast and have small stomachs, so they need small, frequent meals full of good food. WHO advises only breast milk for the first 6 months. From about 6 months, add soft, mashed family foods and keep breastfeeding to 2 years or longer. Start with small amounts and slowly give more, thicker food and more kinds.
How often (WHO): 2 to 3 meals a day for babies of 6 to 8 months; 3 to 4 meals a day for children of 9 to 23 months, plus 1 to 2 snacks if needed. Make porridge thick enough to stay on the spoon, and add something from another group: mashed beans or groundnut paste, an egg, small fish ground into powder, mashed greens or pawpaw. Give the child their own bowl so you can see how much they eat.
Pregnant and breastfeeding women need more good food, not just more staple. Add an extra small meal or snack each day, with iron-rich foods (beans, small fish, eggs, liver, dark greens) eaten with a vitamin C food. Go to all antenatal visits and take only the supplements the clinic gives you.
When a child is sick, WHO advises more drinks and more breastfeeding, and soft favourite foods. After the illness, give extra food to help the child catch up. If a child is not growing well or is very thin or swollen, go to the clinic.
Step by step:
- Check the child's age in months.
- Plan the number of meals for that age.
- Make each meal thick and add another food group.
- For a pregnant or breastfeeding woman: add a snack with an iron-rich food and vitamin C.
Words to know:
- Complementary feeding: giving family foods from about 6 months while breastfeeding continues.
- Snack: a small amount of food between meals, such as a banana, groundnuts or an egg.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Infant and young child feeding
- WHO fact sheet: Anaemia (who is at risk, iron-rich foods, foods that block iron)
Try it now: Plan one day of food for a child of 10 months (for example in Douala or Kumasi) or for a breastfeeding mother. Write each meal and snack and the food groups it covers.
You can now plan a day's meals for a young child or a pregnant or breastfeeding woman that follows WHO advice.

check.q: How many meals a day does WHO advise for a baby of 7 months?
check.why: WHO advises 2 to 3 meals a day at 6 to 8 months, with breastfeeding.

check.q: Which porridge is best for a 9-month-old?
options: Thick porridge with groundnut paste or mashed egg
check.why: Thick porridge with another food group gives more nutrients in a small stomach.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing a weekly meal plan on a budget
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a weekly meal plan and shopping list that fits your budget.
This lesson builds toward: Given your household's size and food budget, you will write a weekly meal plan and shopping list, covering several food groups every day and staying within the budget.
A plan saves money and makes it easier to eat well. Start with your food budget for the week. Then plan the main meals, using cheap staples, beans or small fish most days, and vegetables every day. Plan eggs, meat or chicken for some days if the budget allows.
Repeat meals your family likes, but change the vegetable or the bean so there is variety. Cook beans once and use them in two meals. Plan the child's meals and the snack for a pregnant or breastfeeding woman first, so they are never the ones left out.
From the plan, write the shopping list with your own market prices, add them up and compare with the budget. If you are over, swap a costly food for a cheaper one in the same group, not for nothing. Example (made-up numbers): a family in Nakuru with a weekly budget of KES 2,500 swaps two meat meals for omena and beans to stay within it.
Put the plan on the wall or save a photo on your phone. At the end of the week, check what you spent and what you threw away, and change next week's plan.
Step by step:
- Write your weekly food budget.
- Plan the main meals for seven days with several food groups each day.
- Plan meals for children and pregnant or breastfeeding women first.
- Write the shopping list with your prices and add it up.
- If over budget, swap within the same food group.
Words to know:
- Budget: the amount of money you plan to spend.
- Meal plan: a list of what you will cook for each day.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-week meal plan. For each day list the meals and food groups, with fruit or vegetables daily; mark the foods for any young child or pregnant or breastfeeding woman; write the shopping list with your prices and total it against the budget; and write three habits you will use.
You can now write a weekly meal plan and shopping list that feeds the household well within your budget.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Food groups every day Most days have only a staple, or the groups are named wrongly. Every day has energy, body-building and protective foods, correctly named. Also includes dark green leaves or orange foods and an iron-rich food most days. Balanced meals Vegetables or fruit are missing on some days. Vegetables or fruit every day, and main meals follow the balanced plate. Iron-rich foods are paired with a vitamin C food, and tea is kept between meals. Salt, sugar and safety No habits listed, or they do not cut salt or sugar. Lists one salt habit, one sugar habit and one of the five keys to safer food. Shows the changes in named recipes from the plan. Budget and shopping list No prices, or the total is wrong or over budget with no swap. Shopping list with own market prices and a correct total within the budget. Shows at least one value swap within a food group and notes foods in season. Feeding those who need most No plan for a young child or pregnant or breastfeeding woman in the household. Meals and snacks follow WHO advice for the child's age or for the woman. Thick porridge with another food group, and the right number of meals, are written for each day. Weekly plan Some days are missing. Seven days of meals, ready to put on the wall or phone. Uses leftovers safely and repeats favourites with variety. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Your shopping list is over budget. What is the best change?
options: Swap a costly food for a cheaper one in the same group
check.why: Swapping within a food group keeps the meal balanced and cheaper.

check.q: Whose meals should you plan first?
options: Young children and pregnant or breastfeeding women
check.why: They need the most good food, so they should never be left out.
